content.title: Treasury Market Shrugs Off Jobs Report
content.summary: Treasury yields were choppy after Friday’s mixed jobs report but remained within a fairly narrow range, suggesting the labor-market data has done little to change Wall Street’s expectations for interest-rate cuts.

content.title: Treasury Yields Rebound After Lower-Than-Forecast Jobless Claims
content.summary: Treasury yields rose, reversing Wednesday’s declines, after new data showed that fewer-than-expected Americans filed new claims for unemployment benefits last week.  The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note was recently around 4.

content.title: U.S. Treasury Yields Mixed as Data, Fed's Miran Speech Awaited
content.summary: U.S. Treasury yields were mixed in early trading. Yields on short- and medium-term notes fell, while they are little changed on maturities of 10 years and longer. Thursday's U.S. data will feature weekly jobless claims, ahead of the key December employment report on Friday.

content.title: U.S. Treasury Yields Rise, Focus Shifts to Data
content.summary: U.S. Treasury yields were trading higher in early trade as investors look beyond geopolitical risks. That said, a below-forecast U.S. ISM business manufacturing PMI reading on Monday was a reminder of the fragile outlook, coupled with signals of a cooling labor market.

content.title: Investors Who Bet on a Venezuela Comeback Are Poised for a Payday
content.summary: The ouster of Nicolás Maduro is rewarding investors who spent years betting on a Venezuela comeback.    An estimated $500 million of the debt trades daily, and distressed-debt funds have been buying bonds for a fraction of their face value since select sanctions were eased in 2023.

content.title: Treasury Yields Slip As Market Focus Turns to December Jobs Data
content.summary: Treasury yields declined as investors appeared cautious but not overly concerned about the U.S. capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

content.title: Venezuelan Bonds Rally on Maduro Ouster
content.summary: International debt issued by the Venezuelan government and state-owned oil company PdVSA rallied on Monday after the U.S. ouster of President Nicolás Maduro.  Investors are betting that the Trump administration's capture of Maduro will clear the way for a restructuring of Venezuela's sovereign debt, which the government defaulted on in 2017 after the U.S. imposed sanctions on the Maduro regime.  The sanctions have made it impossible for international investors who lent billions of dollars to Venezuela to negotiate a restructuring.
